skills.name: Define the mole and the Avogadro constant and apply them to atoms, molecules and ions

note.text:
A mole is the amount of a substance that holds as many particles as there are atoms in 12 g of carbon-12. That number is the Avogadro constant, L = 6.02 × 10²³ per mole.
One mole of any substance holds 6.02 × 10²³ particles, whether they are atoms, molecules or ions.
• 1 mol of helium = 6.02 × 10²³ atoms.
• 1 mol of water = 6.02 × 10²³ molecules, but 3 × 6.02 × 10²³ atoms, because each molecule has 3 atoms.
• 1 mol of NaCl gives 2 mol of ions: one of Na⁺ and one of Cl⁻.
Number of particles = moles × L.
The mass of one mole is the molar mass in g/mol, and one mole of any gas fills 22.4 dm³ at s.t.p.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to define the mole and the Avogadro constant, and count particles, atoms and ions in a given amount.
Builds on: Lesson {19} (relative masses) and Form Three the mole of atoms.
Leads to: Lesson {21}, where moles, mass and volume are used together in calculations.

sections.heading: The mole and the Avogadro constant
sections.text:
Chemists work with huge numbers of atoms, so they count them in moles.
A MOLE is the amount of a substance that holds as many particles as there are atoms in {12} g of carbon-{12}. That number is the AVOGADRO CONSTANT, L = {6.02} × {10} to the power {23} per mole.
One mole of any substance holds that many particles:
• {1} mol of helium: {6.02} × {10} to the power {23} atoms;
• {1} mol of carbon dioxide: {6.02} × {10} to the power {23} molecules;
• {1} mol of sodium chloride: {6.02} × {10} to the power {23} formula units, which is {2} mol of ions.
Number of particles = moles × L.

sections.heading: Atoms, molecules and ions
sections.text:
Be careful to say WHICH particle is being counted.
One mole of water, {formula('H2O')}:
• {1} mol of molecules;
• {3} mol of atoms, because each molecule has {2} hydrogen and {1} oxygen;
• {2} mol of hydrogen atoms and {1} mol of oxygen atoms.
One mole of {formula('H2SO4')} holds {7} mol of atoms: {2} of hydrogen, {1} of sulphur and {4} of oxygen.
One mole of {formula('CaCl2')} gives {3} mol of ions: {1} of calcium and {2} of chloride.
Together with the molar mass from Lesson {19}, this links a mass you can weigh to a number of particles you cannot count.

key_words.meaning: the amount of substance holding {6.02} × {10} to the power {23} particles
the group of ions shown by the formula of an ionic compound

mistake.wrong: one mole of water holds {6.02} × {10} to the power {23} atoms
mistake.right: it holds that many MOLECULES, and three times as many atoms
mistake.why: Each water molecule has {3} atoms, so a mole of molecules is {3} mol of atoms.

worked_example.problem: How many molecules, and how many atoms, are there in {n} mol of {formula(F)}?
steps: Number of molecules = moles × L = {n} × {6.02} × {10} to the power {23}.
So the number of atoms is {totalAtoms(F)} × {particles(n)}.

cards.idea: One mole holds {6.02} × {10} to the power {23} particles: the Avogadro constant.
example: {1} mol of helium = {6.02} × {10} to the power {23} atoms
{2} mol of {formula('CO2')} = {1.2} × {10} to the power {24} molecules

cards.idea: A mole of molecules holds more than a mole of atoms: count the atoms in the formula.

check.prompt: How many moles of {E} atoms are there in {n} mol of {formula(F)}?

misconceptions.explain: Each formula unit holds {atomCount(F, E)} atoms of {E}, not one.
Count only the {E} atoms ({atomCount(F, E)}), not all {totalAtoms(F)}.

solution: Each formula unit of {formula(F)} holds {atomCount(F, E)} atoms of {E}.

pick.q: How many atoms are there in one mole of water molecules?
pick.r: Three times the Avogadro number, because each molecule has {3} atoms
w: One third of the Avogadro number
e: That is the number of MOLECULES, not of atoms.
There are {2} hydrogen atoms AND {1} oxygen atom: {3} in all.
There are more atoms than molecules, not fewer.

pick.q: How many ions are there in one mole of sodium chloride, {formula('NaCl')}?
pick.r: Two moles of ions: one of {formula('Na')} and one of {formula('Cl')}
e: Each formula unit gives TWO ions.
{formula('NaCl')} holds only two ions per formula unit.
Sodium chloride is ionic: it is made of ions.
pick.y: {formula('NaCl')} → {formula('Na')} and {formula('Cl')} ions, so a mole of the salt gives {2} mol of ions.

questions.prompt: How many moles of atoms are there in {n} mol of {formula(F)} molecules?

misconceptions.explain: A molecule holds more than one atom: multiply by {totalAtoms(F)}.
Count the ATOMS ({totalAtoms(F)}), not the different elements ({elementCount(F)}).

questions.prompt: How many moles are there in {m} g of {formula(F)}?

misconceptions.explain: Moles = mass ÷ molar mass: divide, do not multiply.
Divide the MASS by the molar mass, not the other way round.

solution: The molar mass of {formula(F)} is {molarMass(F)} g/mol.

questions.prompt: What is the mass, in grams, of {n} mol of {formula(F)}?

misconceptions.explain: Mass = moles × molar mass: multiply, do not divide.
{molarMass(F)} g is the mass of ONE mole; here there are {n} mol.

solution: The molar mass of {formula(F)} is {molarMass(F)} g/mol.
